title: T1588.002 — Obtain Capabilities - Tool
subtitle: Interactive walkthrough of Obtain Capabilities - Tool with the technique-specific attack path and defender evidence.
aria: Attack simulation, step 1 of 8. Planning the toolkit. The attacker lists what the operation needs: a command and control framework, credential theft tools, and ways to move between machines. Tools are faster to buy than to build.

steps.title: Planning the toolkit
steps.caption: The attacker lists what the operation needs: a command and control framework, credential theft tools, and ways to move between machines. Tools are faster to buy than to build.
steps.defender: Nothing is visible. No tool has touched your network yet.

steps.title: Getting cracked tools
steps.caption: The actor buys a cracked Cobalt Strike license on a forum and downloads open-source tools like Mimikatz and LaZagne. Public reporting shows many groups obtained tools this way, from FIN7 to DarkVishnya.
steps.defender: You still see nothing, but the cracked build keeps default traits that researchers already document.

steps.title: Setting up the team server
steps.caption: The actor uploads the toolkit to a rented server, starts the team server, and requests a TLS certificate for the new domain. Certificate transparency logs publish it within minutes.
steps.defender: First visibility: a new certificate for a fresh domain appears in public CT logs. Nothing links it to you yet.

steps.title: Configuring the beacon
steps.caption: The actor edits the malleable profile, the file that tells the beacon how to look and talk. Many buyers keep the defaults, and every default is a marker defenders know.
steps.defender: Nothing on your side yet. But default pipes and certificate traits survive lazy setups, and those are exactly what your rules should watch.

steps.title: Phishing delivers the loader
steps.caption: A phishing mail carries a link to the team server. The loader drops beacon.exe into a user folder and creates its first named pipe. Sysmon sees the file and the pipe at once.
steps.defender: Endpoint logs now hold two events: an executable written to a user path and a pipe named MSSE-1668-server. Together they are a strong signal.

steps.title: Beacon check-in
steps.caption: The beacon calls home over HTTPS. The cracked build uses its default TLS setup, so the IDS flags the client fingerprint and the self-signed certificate of the framework.
steps.defender: IDS and proxy logs hold a Suricata alert and a known default JA3 fingerprint. Pair it with the pipe event from step 5.

steps.title: Credential tools on the host
steps.caption: With session access, the actor runs credential dumping tools such as LaZagne and remote execution with Impacket-style patterns. Process creation logging records the odd command lines.
steps.defender: Process creation events show a known tool pattern on a workstation that should never run it. Process lineage shows how it got there.

steps.title: The SOC joins the dots
steps.caption: The SOC correlates pipe names, the IDS fingerprint, and process lineage into one case. The host is isolated and credentials are reset before ransomware can follow.
steps.defender: Correlation turns three weak signals into a confirmed intrusion. Cracked tools fail here: their defaults survive.
